title: Trafficking (8 February)
hookLine: on Bakhita's day the Church prays against human trafficking

lines: A GIRL TAKEN FROM THE FIELDS.
cards: A little girl in Sudan, out in the fields near her village, is grabbed by strangers and carried off. She's so frightened that, by her own later account, she forgets the name her parents gave her.

Her captors give her a new one: Bakhita. She is sold, and sold again, and she bears the scars. Years later, in Italy, she meets the Canossian sisters, is baptized Josephine, and stays among them for the rest of her life.
This path met her last year. The Church keeps her feast on the eighth of February, and on that day it prays against the trade that took her childhood.

teach.b: First, the name. Bakhita is an Arabic word meaning fortunate, or lucky. Her kidnappers gave it to her.
It's hard to hear that without wincing: a stolen child called the lucky one. And yet Josephine Bakhita kept the name all her life, and the Church honors her by it. Second, the turn.
In Italy, when the family that held her wanted to take her away again, the question of her freedom went before the authorities, and she was recognized as free.

She chose to stay with the sisters, and later became one of them. Her story isn't only about what was done to her. It's about a woman who was owned and then, at last, belonged to herself, and gave herself to God.
Trafficking is the buying, selling, moving or holding of people by force, fraud or coercion, for labor, for sex, for profit. It isn't only a story from another century.
It happens in fields and kitchens, on fishing boats, in nail salons and apartments, sometimes in plain sight. Fourth, the Church's response.

teach.h: A DAY OF PRAYER ON HER FEAST.
teach.b: On Bakhita's feast the Church keeps a day of prayer and reflection against trafficking, and religious sisters run shelters and outreach for survivors.

Underneath is Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, where he reads from Isaiah that he has been sent "to preach deliverance to the captives." Catholic teaching holds that a person can never be property. Not for any price.

how: On 8 February, the feast of Saint Josephine Bakhita, Catholics keep a day of prayer and reflection against human trafficking, and religious sisters and Catholic charities run shelters, outreach and awareness work for survivors.

o: heavy traffic on the roads into a big city
smuggling goods like drugs across borders
buying, selling or holding people by force

p: her feast, a day of prayer

s: Bakhita was the name her parents gave her
her captors gave it to her; by her own account she had forgotten her birth name.
trafficking is only a story from another century
it happens today, in fields, kitchens, boats and apartments, sometimes in plain sight.
once recognized as free, Bakhita chose to stay with the sisters
she was baptized Josephine and later became a Canossian sister.

games.q: you're Bakhita in Italy. the family that held you wants to take you away again. the authorities say you're free. what do you do?
o: go with the family; it's all you've known.
stay with the sisters, by your own choice.
games.why: she stayed with the Canossian sisters, was baptized Josephine, and later became one of them.

practice: Hold one sign that anti-trafficking groups often point to: someone not allowed to keep their own passport or ID, because a boss keeps it, or a worker who owes a debt they can never seem to pay off.
You're not looking to accuse anyone; you're learning to see. If you pray, ask Saint Josephine Bakhita to pray for those held captive; if you don't, simply remember her name.

wordCard.voice: Trafficking. The buying, selling and holding of people by force or fraud, which the Church prays against on Bakhita's feast. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: fortunate, or lucky, the name her kidnappers gave her, which she kept all her life.

carryVoice: Your line: no one for sale. If you or someone near you is in danger, call local emergency help, or 988 in the US. See you tomorrow.
